lead.title: The child's routine becomes the household's hardest hire, as the travelling nanny turns into a career of her own
lead.standfirst: Multi-residence families and burned-out live-in staff are together reshaping private childcare into rotating teams, and the pay is following the pressure.
lead.body:
For a generation, the private nanny was a single figure who lived where the family lived and moved when the family moved. That model is quietly breaking. Agencies serving ultra-high-net-worth households now report that the fastest-growing brief is not the live-in nanny at all but the rota nanny, a professional who works a fixed cycle, typically two weeks on followed by two weeks off, so that the child always has continuity of care while no single person carries the whole year alone. The change is being driven from two directions at once. Families increasingly run three or four residences and expect childcare to travel with them across time zones. At the same time, experienced candidates have started to refuse the classic single-nanny arrangement outright, having watched colleagues burn out inside it.

The money has moved with the pressure. In the strongest markets a senior nanny is no longer a modest domestic line. Switzerland now leads the world on pay, with packages reported around USD 144,000, and the United States follows close behind at roughly USD 120,000, rising in New York to elite packages of USD 150,000 to USD 180,000 and beyond. A senior rota position based in Dubai will often carry a package worth from 80,000 to more than 120,000 pounds once accommodation and flights are counted. These are not pin money figures. They sit alongside the salaries of the estate managers and private chefs who run the same houses, and they are negotiated with the same seriousness.

Above the nanny sits the governess, and here the household is buying something closer to education than to care. A newly qualified governess with a teaching qualification and one or two years in a private house earns from 35,000 to 45,000 pounds gross. With three to five years behind her the range moves to between 45,000 and 65,000 pounds. The senior governess who is genuinely bilingual and willing to live out of a suitcase across several countries commands 65,000 pounds and upward, frequently past 90,000. What the family is paying for is fluency, discretion and the ability to hold a child's schooling together while the household itself is in motion.

For the person who runs the house, this is a structural shift rather than a passing fashion. A rota model means two or three childcare professionals per child rather than one, each with a contract, a travel schedule, a handover protocol and a claim on the family calendar. The house manager becomes the person who designs those cycles, keeps the handovers seamless and makes sure that the child never feels the seam between one carer leaving and the next arriving. The nursery has become, in effect, a small department, and someone has to run it.
lead.why: Childcare is moving from a single trusted figure to a managed rotating team, and the house manager is increasingly the one who designs the cycle, writes the handover and holds the continuity together.

articles.title: The family office stops being run by the family, and the outside professional inherits the keys
articles.body:
The family office was born as an intimate thing, a trusted relative or a long-serving adviser looking after one household's fortune. It is becoming an institution. Deloitte's global research puts the assets managed by single family offices on a path to rise by roughly 73 per cent, from about USD 3.1 trillion today to some USD 5.4 trillion by 2030, a scale that no relative can steward on instinct alone. As the money grows, so does the machinery around it, and with the machinery comes the professional.

The most telling number is not about assets but about who is in charge. Today only around 35 per cent of family office heads are non-family professionals. After the coming wave of generational handovers, Deloitte expects that figure to reach close to 49 per cent, meaning that in roughly half of these houses the person setting strategy will no longer share the family's surname. Four in ten family offices say they intend to add staff, and a growing share of that hiring is aimed squarely at outside expertise rather than promotion from within the family circle.

That professionalisation reshapes the household as a place to work. A family office run by an outside chief executive brings governance, written policies, defined reporting lines and human resources discipline into a world that used to run on personal loyalty and unspoken understanding. For the private staff who sit near the family, the house manager, the principal's assistant, the estate team, this can be steadying. Roles are written down, pay is benchmarked and progression becomes legible. It can also be colder. The handshake is replaced by the contract, and the person who once answered only to the principal now answers to a structure.

The direction of travel is clear enough. The private household is being absorbed into something that looks more like a small institution each year, with the family office as its head office and the residences as its operations. Whoever serves the family will increasingly serve it through that structure, and the ability to work inside a professional chain of command, not merely to please one person, becomes part of the craft.
articles.why: As outside executives take charge of family offices, private staff increasingly report into professional structures rather than to the principal alone, and fluency in governance becomes as valuable as personal trust.
articles.src: Deloitte Private, Family Office Insights Series

articles.title: The residence now arrives with a name on the door, and service is written into the deeds
articles.body:
One of the clearest signals of how the very wealthy now want to live is the branded residence, a private home attached to a hotel or fashion name and sold with that name's service built in. Savills counts the number of branded residence schemes rising from 764 at the end of 2024 to around 910 by the close of 2025, a growth rate of about 19 per cent in a single year. With 837 further projects contracted through 2032, the total pipeline points toward some 1,747 schemes. The map is widening with the numbers, spanning more than 90 countries, of which 25 are seeing their first branded development.

Buyers pay handsomely for the badge. A branded home carries a global average price premium of about 33 per cent over comparable unbranded stock, rising to roughly 39 per cent in resort locations. Part of that premium is prestige, but a large part is service. At the top of the market the names doing the defining are the ones a private principal already knows, Aman, Auberge, Montage and Kerzner in the ultra-luxury tier, with Four Seasons the single most influential operator, followed closely by Mandarin Oriental and Aman. Marriott and Accor lead on sheer scale, each carrying portfolios of more than 35 brands.

What the buyer is really purchasing is a household that comes pre-staffed. Housekeeping, security, maintenance and concierge arrive with the deeds, delivered to a hotel standard and charged through service fees. For a time-poor family with several homes, that is the appeal, a residence that runs itself the moment they walk in and keeps running when they leave.

For the private service profession this cuts two ways. The branded residence can absorb functions that a family once hired directly, thinning the traditional in-house team in favour of a building's shared staff. It also creates a large new field of employment inside those buildings, and it raises the bar for the private house manager who still runs a family's own estate, because the family now measures home against the seamless standard of a five-star operator, and expects to feel no difference.
articles.why: Branded residences fold housekeeping, security and concierge into the building, reshaping where private staff are employed and setting a hotel-grade benchmark that in-house teams are now judged against.

articles.title: Private flying sets fresh records, and the new fortune coming out of the markets is doing the flying
articles.body:
Private aviation has stopped being described as a recovery and is now simply setting records. Charter and fractional flight totals for 2026 are running about 42 per cent above their 2019 level, and the momentum has not faded with the summer. Late in July, a 12 per cent year-on-year jump in United States private jet departures lifted worldwide flights to a roughly 7 per cent gain, with the flight-tracking analysts at WingX noting that the four-week trend of about 7 per cent is outpacing the global year-to-date figure of around 5 per cent. Growth is showing up across every category at once, from owner flights to fractional ownership to on-demand charter.

The engine behind the numbers is new wealth. Analysts point to a surge of initial public offerings and a growing population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals as the clearest drivers of demand, with Jefferies reporting that 2026 flotation proceeds are running at nearly three times the level of the previous year. When a founder or an early employee turns paper worth into cash, one of the first purchases is mobility, and the correlation between flotation activity and jet deliveries is strong. Fresh money quite literally takes to the air.

The operators are building for it. NetJets, the largest fractional operator, has said it has pre-sold more than half of the aircraft deliveries it expects next year, and plans to take on the order of 100 aircraft this year and again the year after. That is a company betting real capital that the demand is structural rather than a passing spike, and its order commitments ripple through the whole manufacturing chain.

For the concierge and the house manager, this is the practical texture of the job. A principal whose wealth is newly liquid flies more, plans later and expects the machine on the tarmac when the diary shifts. Managing that means holding relationships with fractional providers and charter brokers, understanding lead times that lengthen as the fleet fills, and treating aviation as a standing logistical discipline rather than an occasional booking.
articles.why: New wealth from public offerings is flying more and planning later, which puts a premium on the house manager who treats aviation as a standing relationship with operators rather than a one-off booking.

articles.title: Fine wine settles at the floor, and the patient cellar becomes a buyer's advantage
articles.body:
After the euphoria of the early decade, fine wine has spent two years coming back to earth, and 2026 is the year it has settled there. The Liv-ex Fine Wine Investables Index, which tracks the blue-chip end of the cellar, sits roughly 25 per cent below its 2022 peak, with prices across many leading regions and vintages hovering near five-year lows. Liv-ex itself expects the market to bump along the bottom through the year, describing the moment not as a crash but as the start of a slow recovery, and openly framing it as an opening for buyers who were priced out at the top.

The correction has been broad. Bordeaux and Burgundy, the two anchors of any serious collection, have both given ground, and the speculative premium that once attached to the most fashionable Burgundy labels has thinned considerably. What remains valued, and what still trades, is provenance. In a soft market the buyer can afford to be exacting, and impeccable storage history and clean documentation have become the difference between a wine that sells and one that lingers. Condition is now the currency.

For the household this is less an investment note than a matter of cultural fluency and cellar management. A family cellar bought at the peak may be showing a paper loss, and the person who keeps the records should understand why without alarm. A patient household, by contrast, can build depth at prices unseen in years, provided it buys on provenance rather than label and stores the wine properly.

The craft point is quiet but real. Whoever runs the cellar is expected to know the market well enough to advise on when to hold, when to drink and when a bottle is worth insuring rather than opening, and to speak about it with the ease of someone who belongs in the room. In a buyer's market that fluency is worth more, not less.
articles.why: A soft fine wine market rewards the household that buys on provenance and stores with discipline, and it raises the value of a cellar keeper who can advise with genuine fluency rather than follow fashion.

briefs.t: A record year for moving
briefs.b: Henley & Partners forecasts that as many as 165,000 millionaires will relocate in 2026, the largest wealth migration it has recorded. The United Arab Emirates remains the leading destination, with Singapore, Italy, Switzerland and Greece rising, while the United Kingdom, Germany and France are named among those losing ground.

briefs.t: The saleroom finds its feet
briefs.b: Global auction sales at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips rose about 70 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, to some USD 6.8 billion including fees, the best first half since 2022. Sotheby's reported total turnover of USD 4.4 billion, an all-time high, and luxury collectibles climbed 25 per cent, with memorabilia up a striking 308 per cent.

briefs.t: London runs short of butlers
briefs.b: The formal butler remains one of the hardest roles to fill in London, with pay reported up by 20 to 25 per cent since 2022 and demand growing by about 9 per cent a year. Experienced housekeepers are described as genuinely scarce across the major markets, keeping the whole senior household team in a candidate's position.

briefs.t: Fewer yachts, but bigger
briefs.b: BOAT International's Global Order Book lists 1,093 yachts in build or on order over 24 metres, with unit numbers down for a second straight year even as the average length under construction reaches a record 40.8 metres. Azimut Benetti tops the order book for a 26th successive year. The fleet is consolidating into fewer, larger vessels that demand larger and better-paid crews.

lead.title: Health moves into the household, and the person who runs the house is asked to run the longevity plan
lead.standfirst: As the very wealthy put longevity at the centre of their planning, the coordination of doctors, clinics and recovery is quietly becoming a task for the estate, not just the family office.
lead.body:
Bank of America's 2025 Study of Wealthy Americans found that longer lives and an accelerating transfer of wealth are together making family finances more complex, with more members, more decades and more moving parts to hold in view at once. The headline is financial, but the consequence lands squarely inside the house. When a principal expects to live and work well into a tenth decade, the calendar fills not only with meetings and travel but with scans, specialists, recovery windows and the discreet logistics of keeping a body in working order.

A parallel shift is visible in the market for private medicine. Longevity clinics, offering full-body imaging, hormonal and metabolic panels, sleep optimisation and preventative screening, have moved from the fringe to the centre of how many ultra-high-net-worth individuals now think about their time. Health has become a status good in its own right, and the appointments are as jealously guarded as any board seat. What used to be an annual physical is now a standing programme, with data, protocols and a small roster of practitioners attached to it.

None of this coordinates itself. Increasingly it is the house manager, the private personal assistant or the family concierge who books the imaging slot in one city and the consultant in another, who moves the recovery week around the travel schedule, who briefs a new private nurse and who keeps the medical file as carefully as the wine cellar log. The work sits at the intersection of the most sensitive information in the household and the most unforgiving logistics, and it rewards absolute discretion.

The same theme is reshaping the clubs the wealthy join. Wellness suites, longevity programmes and resident medical experts are now central to what a modern private membership is expected to deliver, a sign of where attention and spending are moving. For anyone entering private service, the message is plain. Fluency in the language of health, from the vocabulary of a longevity protocol to the etiquette of handling a medical record, is fast becoming part of the core skill set, not a specialism at the edge of it.
lead.why: The house is being asked to manage the principal's health as carefully as the estate. Comfort with medical logistics and absolute discretion around health data are becoming central to senior private roles.
lead.src: Bank of America Private Bank; InsideHook

articles.title: The Gulf starts hiring the people who run London and New York houses, and pay follows them east
articles.body:
The Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026 places housekeepers, private chefs, nannies and estate managers at the top of demand across the United States, with the number of qualified candidates growing far more slowly than the number of houses that need them. That gap alone would push pay upward. What is new is where the competition now comes from.

The report singles out Dubai and other low-tax jurisdictions as active buyers of English-speaking senior staff, drawing experienced house managers and estate managers away from established markets in London and the United States. For a principal in the Gulf, the appeal is obvious. Tax-free packages, a fast-growing base of resident wealth and a preference for staff who can move seamlessly between cultures make a seasoned London-trained house manager a prize worth paying for.

The effect on wages is straightforward. A senior estate or house manager running multiple properties now commonly commands a six-figure salary, and employers are offering increases above the general market simply to keep the people they already have. The counter-offer, once unusual, has become a standard feature of any resignation conversation at the top of the profession.

Training sits underneath all of it. The most sought-after profile remains the hybrid, a former butler who has grown into house management, or a house manager with formal service training behind them, often from a name such as The Savoy or Claridge's. As demand spreads geographically, that formal grounding becomes the credential that travels, the thing that lets a candidate command a Gulf package as readily as a London one.

For those entering the field, the map has widened. The best households are no longer only in a handful of Western cities, and the career now runs across jurisdictions, currencies and climates. Mobility, cultural range and a portable qualification are becoming as valuable as the length of a reference.
articles.why: The competition for senior staff has gone global, and the Gulf is now bidding directly for London and New York talent. Formal training and willingness to relocate are becoming the levers that set a career apart.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026

articles.title: Prime property rises again across the world, and the surprise of the year is Tokyo
articles.body:
Knight Frank's Prime International Residential Index, the firm's measure of luxury home values across 100 of the world's leading markets, rose by 3.2 per cent on average through 2025, a shade below the 3.6 per cent recorded the year before but still comfortably positive. Of the 100 markets tracked, 73 rose in value and 24 fell, a spread that points to a market climbing steadily rather than surging.

The standout was Tokyo, where prime values jumped by 58.5 per cent. A weak yen turned Japanese trophy homes into an obvious value play for buyers holding dollars, and demand for new-build luxury in the capital followed the currency. It is a reminder that in prime property the exchange rate can matter as much as the address, and that a shift in currency can redraw the map of where the wealthy choose to buy.

Dubai extended its run with a 25.1 per cent rise, keeping its place as the most active super-prime hub in the world and reinforcing the pull that is also drawing staff and capital to the Gulf. The Middle East was the strongest region overall, up 9.4 per cent, as buyers continued to concentrate on a small number of gateway cities where liquidity and lifestyle meet.

For the household, index movements are never abstract. They signal where principals are buying, and therefore where new houses will need to be opened, staffed and run. A surge in a given city tends to be followed, a season or two later, by a wave of hiring, refurbishment and the quiet work of standing up a fully functioning residence from an empty shell.
articles.why: The wealth map is redrawn by prime-property flows, and staff follow the houses. A city that spikes on the index today is often a city hiring house managers and opening residences tomorrow.

articles.title: The order books are full and the factories accelerate, as a tax rule pulls buyers forward
articles.body:
The private aviation cycle has turned firmly towards production. Gulfstream handed over 158 aircraft in 2025, 136 of them large-cabin, while Bombardier delivered 157, including 86 large jets. Behind those numbers sit order books that remain deep by any historical measure, with Bombardier reporting a backlog of 17.5 billion dollars and Gulfstream 15.5 billion dollars, the latter with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.2, meaning new orders are still arriving faster than aircraft leave the line.

Across the industry the picture is the same. Manufacturer backlogs were estimated at more than 55 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2025, up 8.4 per cent on the year before. The flagship models tell the story of the ramp. The Gulfstream G700 recorded 64 deliveries in 2025 and is expected to exceed 80 in 2026, while Bombardier's Global 8000 enters full production this year and Gulfstream's new G400 begins reaching customers.

One policy lever is pulling demand forward. In the United States, the return of 100 per cent bonus depreciation lets qualifying buyers write off much of an aircraft's cost against tax in the year of purchase, a powerful incentive to commit now rather than later. Combined with a growing base of ultra-wealthy owners, it keeps the pressure on delivery slots and lengthens the wait for the most sought-after cabins.

For the concierge and the estate that manages a principal's movement, the consequence is practical. New aircraft mean new crews, new maintenance relationships and, often, a rethink of how a household charters versus owns. A tighter delivery pipeline also means that access, not price, is frequently the binding constraint, and the households that plan their flying furthest ahead are the ones that keep their options open.
articles.why: Aircraft are the concierge's logistical backbone, and a full order book changes the calculus of owning versus chartering. Long waits for new jets put a premium on planning a principal's movement well in advance.

articles.title: Coloured diamonds carry the salerooms, and the rarest stones sell whatever the mood
articles.body:
The high jewellery auctions have delivered a run of firm results, and the pattern within them is clear. Rare coloured diamonds, and blue stones above all, are setting the pace. At Christie's Magnificent Jewels in New York, the sale reached 49.7 million dollars with every lot sold. The Azure Blue, a 31.62-carat pear-shaped fancy blue diamond of VVS1 clarity, led at 8.4 million dollars, closely followed by a 5.04-carat marquise-shaped fancy vivid blue at 8.2 million dollars.

Sotheby's told a similar story. A 10.02-carat fancy intense blue diamond of VS2 clarity sold for 8.7 million dollars, heading a 43.4 million dollar sale with a 98 per cent sell-through rate. A separate high jewellery auction in New York took 31.4 million dollars with 95 per cent of lots sold, described as the house's strongest sell-through for a various-owner jewellery sale in the city. When 95 to 100 per cent of a room finds a buyer, the market is not merely holding, it is confident.

The appetite is concentrated at the top. Bidders are paying up for size, saturation of colour and impeccable provenance, and they are largely unmoved by wider economic noise when a stone is genuinely rare. The middle of the market is quieter, but the exceptional lot behaves as if there were no cycle at all.

For those who serve collectors, the saleroom is part of the world they must read fluently. A principal who buys at this level expects the people around them to understand what a coloured diamond is, why provenance moves a price and how a jewel is stored, insured, transported and worn. Cultural literacy of this kind, the ability to speak the language of the collection, is quietly part of the modern brief.
articles.why: Serving a collector demands fluency in what they buy and why. Knowing how a jewel is valued, insured and moved is part of the cultural range expected of senior household and concierge staff.

articles.title: Off the Riviera, a whole island is turned into one discreet village
articles.body:
Among the year's more unusual openings, Zannier is transforming the Ile de Bendor, a small private island off the coast of Bandol on the French Riviera, into a single low-key retreat. Rather than a conventional resort, the project is arranged as roughly 93 villas and suites laid out to resemble a secluded Provencal village, with the intent of privacy and discretion rather than spectacle.

The appeal for a well-served guest is the combination of seclusion and proximity. The island sits within easy reach of the mainland and the wider Riviera, yet its separateness delivers the quiet and control that a principal increasingly values, a place where movement can be managed and interruption designed out.

For the private world, formats like this matter because they mirror how the wealthy prefer to travel. The direction of luxury hospitality is towards villas rather than rooms, towards space that can be taken over rather than shared, and towards a level of privacy that behaves more like a borrowed estate than a hotel. Understanding that shift, and knowing which properties can genuinely deliver it, is part of the concierge's working knowledge.
articles.why: A single, well-chosen private-island retreat shows where discerning travel is heading, towards villas and takeover privacy rather than conventional rooms. Knowing which properties truly deliver seclusion is core concierge knowledge.

briefs.t: Crew pay keeps climbing at sea
briefs.b: Superyacht crew salaries have risen by roughly 8 to 12 per cent since 2023, driven by persistent shortages and inflation, according to 2026 crew salary guides. Chief engineers and professional chefs remain the hardest berths to fill, with demand for qualified people still outrunning supply.

briefs.t: Clubs rebuild around longevity
briefs.b: A younger generation of billionaires and founders is reshaping the private members club, pushing wellness suites, longevity programmes and resident medical experts to the centre of the membership. The shift signals where attention and spending among the very wealthy are moving.

briefs.t: Business jet backlogs top USD 55bn
briefs.b: Manufacturer order backlogs across business aviation were estimated at more than 55 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2025, up 8.4 per cent year on year. The depth of the books points to full factories and long waits for the most in-demand cabins well into 2026.

briefs.t: A Mellon blue heads to the block
briefs.b: Christie's is set to offer the Mellon Blue, a 9.51-carat blue diamond once owned by the American horticulturalist and philanthropist Bunny Mellon, with an estimate of 20 to 30 million dollars. Provenance of this order tends to draw the deepest bidding, whatever the wider market is doing.

lead.title: The saleroom rebounds, and the family collection quietly becomes a credit line
lead.standfirst: Christie's and Sotheby's have posted their strongest first half in years, and the most consequential detail sits not in the hammer prices but in the lending books built around them.
lead.body: Both houses published half year figures on 15 July. Christie's reported revenue of USD 4.5 billion, with public auction sales up 71 per cent year on year at USD 3.5 billion and a sell-through rate of 91 per cent by lot, against 87 per cent in 2025. Sotheby's public auction sales reached USD 3.4 billion, up 59 per cent, with total turnover of USD 4.4 billion including a record USD 826 million in private sales, an all-time high for the house. The single largest collection sold so far this year was that of the publisher S. I. Newhouse, which totalled USD 630.8 million in New York in May and produced two of the year's three highest prices, Jackson Pollock's Number 7A at USD 181.2 million and Constantin Brancusi's Danaide at USD 107.6 million. In June the Lewis collection made USD 406.2 million in London, the highest value sale of Impressionist, Modern and contemporary art ever staged in Europe. The recovery has been carried by trophy material and by what the trade calls, without much affection, the luxury genre: watches, jewellery, cars, handbags, memorabilia. At Christie's that category alone reached USD 539 million, up 15 per cent, and the collection of the businessman Jim Irsay made USD 105.2 million across five auctions closing on 6 July, the highest total ever recorded for a memorabilia collection. Both houses describe luxury as the entry point for a younger client. Christie's says 47 per cent of its new clients this year are Millennial or Generation Z, and that 85 per cent of bids came in online. The structural story is financing. Sotheby's completed a USD 900 million securitisation in January, the ArtFi Master Trust Series 2026-1, bundling art-backed loans into tradable notes sold to institutional investors. For the first time the issuance also included loans secured against collectible cars. Christie's, which opened its art financing arm five years ago, now lends against cars, handbags, watches and increasingly wine. Its chief executive is explicit that many borrowers are not short of capital, they are simply optimising how they use it, and frequently reinvest the proceeds in more art. For the household this changes what a collection is. A picture on a wall that also secures a loan is no longer only an object to be insured, hung and dusted. It is a financial instrument with covenants attached, and its condition, location, provenance file and valuation history acquire a second life inside the family's balance sheet. Loan agreements can restrict where a work may travel, who may handle it and how it must be stored. The person who signs for the crate is now, in practice, part of a credit arrangement.
lead.why: When a collection is pledged as collateral, the accuracy of the house inventory, condition reports and loan documentation stops being an administrative nicety and becomes a financial control. Whoever manages the residence needs to know which works are encumbered before agreeing to move one.

articles.title: The estate manager's pay keeps climbing, because almost nobody holds all three skills at once
articles.body:
The 2026 salary guides published by the private staffing agencies converge on a wide and rising band. In the United States estate managers are quoted from USD 85,000 to USD 250,000, with experienced candidates on base salaries of USD 150,000 to USD 200,000. By market, New York runs from USD 120,000 to USD 180,000, the Hamptons from USD 130,000 to USD 190,000 and Palm Beach from USD 110,000 to USD 160,000. In the United Kingdom the equivalent posts are quoted from GBP 110,000 to GBP 220,000 and above, with the spread driven by the scale of the estate, the headcount reporting in, the size of the budget under authority and whether the role covers one property or several.

The demand side explains the drift upward. Agencies report estate manager searches growing about 16 per cent year on year, and estate management now accounts for roughly one in ten client requests in the United States. The driver is portfolio ownership: families are acquiring additional residences across jurisdictions, and each new address adds a payroll, a contractor list, a security posture and a compliance burden that somebody has to hold.

The constraint is not enthusiasm but the shape of the profile. The brief that agencies are asked to fill combines three competences that rarely sit in one person. First, security literacy, meaning the ability to specify and supervise a protection detail, a surveillance system and a travel protocol without outsourcing judgement entirely. Second, technical command of building systems, from plant rooms and pool infrastructure to networks, access control and increasingly the automation layer that ties them together. Third, genuine management of people, budgets and vendors across multiple sites and time zones.

Most candidates arrive strong in one of the three and passable in a second. The market is therefore paying a premium for the rare third leg rather than for seniority as such, which is why two candidates with identical years of service can be quoted seventy thousand dollars apart. For anyone building a career in private service, the practical implication is that breadth now compounds faster than tenure.
articles.why: The pay gap in this market is a skills gap, not a seniority gap. Deliberately acquiring the weakest of the three competences, usually the technical or the security side, is the most direct route to the top of the published band.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet International, household staff salary guide 2026

articles.title: The family office learns to write down what it pays, and the first hire after a liquidity event is settled
articles.body:
A programme convened by the law firm Katten on 6 May, with Botoff Consulting and the search firm Mack International, set out where family office pay is heading in the second half of 2026. Total direct compensation for both executives and staff has risen meaningfully year on year. The discretionary bonus is giving way to structured annual incentive plans built on individual performance, organisational performance and investment performance, in that order, a sequence that matters because it signals that portfolio return is no longer accepted as the sole measure of a professional's value.

On the supply side, Mack International describes a large uptick in activity, driven by newly created offices and by a wave of succession as principals from the baby boomer generation step back. Experienced talent is not keeping pace. The chief financial officer is currently the hardest seat to fill, because strategic and tax-oriented professionals with estate planning experience are exceptionally scarce, and more than a third of offices in Botoff's 2026 compensation and talent planning survey reported recruiting difficulty in the past year, with the largest offices reporting the most.

The liveliest exchange concerned a practical question: after a liquidity event, who should the family hire first. The recommendation was a family office leader or a chief financial officer, and specifically not a chief investment officer, since a CIO accustomed to reporting directly to the family creates friction when a chief executive is later placed above them. Bringing across a trusted advisor from the sold operating company was flagged as a common source of dysfunction within a couple of years, because running a business and serving as a professional manager to a principal are different disciplines. Build the scaffolding, the panel argued, before pursuing investment hires.

The era of the wink and a nod arrangement is closing. Professionals recruited from institutional backgrounds now expect transparency, documentation and a stated compensation philosophy, and families are increasingly recruiting directly from other family offices. Compensation represents the dominant share of family office operating cost, and the guidance is to re-examine pay structures every two to three years and incentive plans annually.
articles.why: The same formalisation is arriving in the household. Where the family office writes down its compensation philosophy, the house eventually writes down its job descriptions, review cycles and bonus criteria, and vague arrangements become harder to defend.

articles.title: The order book thins for a second year, and Italy now builds more than half the fleet
articles.body:
The 2026 Global Order Book compiled by BOAT International records 1,093 yachts of 24 metres and above on order or in build, down from 1,138 in the 2025 edition. It is the second consecutive annual decline by unit count, and it is not a story of weakening demand so much as of consolidation: fewer hulls, bigger boats, longer waits.

Italy's dominance has hardened. Italian yards account for 568 units, roughly 52 per cent of the entire order book. The Azimut Benetti group leads the rankings for a twenty-sixth consecutive year, with Sanlorenzo, including its sister brand Nautor Swan, in second place at 130 yachts and 4,698 metres of combined length. The concentration means that a large share of the world's private fleet is now being built within a few hundred kilometres of the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic coasts, with the supply chain, the refit capacity and the specialist labour clustered accordingly.

The practical consequence is scheduling. Most established yards cannot deliver a new build before 2028 at the earliest, and at the top-tier German and Dutch builders the wait extends three to four years. A first-time owner entering the market in 2026 is therefore not choosing between yards so much as between three routes: buy an existing hull on the brokerage market and take delivery now, take a slot at a mid-tier yard with available capacity, or wait several seasons for the yard actually wanted.

For the shore side of a household this reshapes the calendar. A build slot secured today commits the family, and the staff who serve it, to a specification frozen years before the boat floats. Interiors, crew accommodation, tender arrangements and the stowage that determines whether a season runs smoothly are decided at a point when the family's travel pattern may look quite different from the one it will have on delivery.
articles.why: Long lead times move the useful conversation forward by years. The person who will run the guest programme has more influence at the specification stage than at any point afterwards, and that stage is now happening well before delivery.

articles.title: The relocation is decided by the tax adviser and executed by the school registrar
articles.body:
Dubai's private school system now exceeds 210 institutions across six major curricula, with annual fees running from about AED 30,000 to AED 120,000. Several new campuses open for the 2026 to 2027 academic year, among them Harrow International School Dubai, and existing schools are expanding capacity. The build-out is a direct response to arrivals: the emirate has absorbed a sustained inflow of internationally mobile families, accelerated in the British case by the ending of the non-domicile regime in April 2025.

The sequence of a family relocation is rarely the one described in the press. The tax position may be settled in a single meeting, and the property acquired within a season. The schooling is what actually determines the date of the move, because places in the sought-after schools are finite, admission cycles are fixed, and a family with three children of different ages frequently cannot place them all in one institution in the same year. Assessments, entrance testing and waiting lists compress the window, and the academic calendar, not the fiscal one, sets the deadline.

This is why private tutors are engaged so early in the process. Families moving from one curriculum to another, typically English national curriculum to International Baccalaureate or an American programme, use tutoring to bridge the gap before assessment rather than after arrival, and in some cases a tutor travels with the family for a transitional year while places are secured. The tutor becomes, briefly, the most operationally significant member of the household.

Dubai's wider private infrastructure has matured in step. The city now supports a genuine ecosystem of members' clubs rather than the handful of hotel-adjacent rooms that existed a few years ago, which matters because a family relocating without an existing social network needs somewhere to reconstruct one.
articles.why: In a relocation the household staff usually own the school logistics: assessment dates, uniform lists, transport, medical records, transitional tutoring. Getting the academic calendar into the family's planning early is one of the most visible contributions the role makes.

articles.title: On Paraga Beach, a Parisian house tries the Cyclades
articles.body:
Fouquet's has opened on the southern coast of Mykonos at Paraga Beach, taking the French group beyond its Paris and Riviera base. The property runs to 61 suites and three villas, built in a contemporary reading of Cycladic architecture, with indoor and outdoor pools, a spa operated in partnership with Dr Barbara Sturm and a basketball court cut directly into the rock.

The villa component is the part worth noting. On an island where the private rental market has long outcompeted hotels for the largest parties, a branded house is selling the combination that families increasingly want: the privacy and space of a villa with the service infrastructure, kitchen and security of a hotel behind it. That combination has become the standard brief for a summer in the Aegean, and it is why so much of the new inventory across the Cyclades is being built as suites with pools rather than conventional rooms.

For anyone arranging a Mediterranean summer, the operational point is that inventory of this kind is thin and moves early. First-release rates on 2026 debuts have gone quickly, and the multi-bedroom units are typically committed well before the season opens.
articles.why: Knowing which properties can absorb a whole family under one roof, with a private pool and a kitchen that can be used, saves a great deal of negotiation later. The distinction between a suite and a genuinely private house is the one the principal will notice.

briefs.t: Art-backed lending is institutionalised, and now includes cars
briefs.b: Sotheby's completed a USD 900 million securitisation in January, the ArtFi Master Trust Series 2026-1, which the house describes as significantly oversubscribed. It bundles art-backed loans into tradable notes sold to institutional investors, and for the first time included loans secured against collectible cars. The house frames the investor appetite as evidence that art is settling into mainstream wealth management rather than sitting beside it.

briefs.t: The average watch bidder now spends USD 129,000
briefs.b: Average spend per watch bidder at Sotheby's is up around 60 per cent year on year, at USD 129,000, and Millennials and Generation Z now account for roughly one third of watch bidders. The house reports the demand shifting toward independent makers such as F. P. Journe, Simon Brette and Rexhep Rexhepi, and describes the buying as less speculative than in the pre-pandemic period.

briefs.t: Seventy per cent of family offices now invest directly
briefs.b: Roughly 70 per cent of family offices make direct private investments, and 83 per cent of those deals are structured as co-investments rather than solo commitments. The pattern explains a good deal of the recruitment pressure on investment and finance staff, since direct dealing requires diligence capacity that an outsourced model does not.

briefs.t: A projected 165,000 millionaires will move country this year
briefs.b: Henley & Partners projects 165,000 high-net-worth individuals will relocate internationally during 2026, a 16 per cent increase on the record 142,000 moves recorded in 2025. Singapore, Italy, Switzerland, Greece, Hong Kong and New Zealand are named among the strongest destinations, while the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Norway and South Korea face growing competitive pressure.

lead.title: Security becomes a department of the house, with its own pay scales, headcount and shortages
lead.standfirst: The 2026 protective benchmarks put a detail agent at USD 128,000 median base, and a family of four under continuous coverage at an annual payroll of USD 1.8m to 2.4m.
lead.body:
Close protection is no longer a service bought in for big journeys, it has become a permanent function of the private house. The 2026 compensation benchmarks for the US market place the executive protection agent at USD 128,000 median base, the detail leader at USD 185,000, and the director of security at USD 230,000. Total compensation adds a multiple of 1.20 to 1.45 times base for the agent, and 1.30 to 1.65 times for the director, including bonus, deferred compensation and programme management incentives.

The question families ask has changed in kind. It is no longer what an agent costs, but how many agents are required, which is a headcount calculation closer to running a hotel department than to hiring a bodyguard. Continuous coverage of a single principal in a static residence needs a minimum of 5 to 6 agents, and 6 to 8 to absorb training, holidays and unplanned absence. A principal travelling continuously needs 8 to 12 agents across the residential detail, the travelling sub-team and advance work. A family of four under continuous coverage needs 12 to 16 agents, an annual payroll of USD 1.8m to 2.4m in baseline US markets, rising above USD 3m in New York or Aspen.

Geography adds its own multipliers. Aspen leads at 1.50 to 1.55 times base with the thinnest qualified pool of any market, ahead of New York, the Hamptons, San Francisco and Geneva at 1.40, then Greenwich, Palm Beach and Monaco at 1.35. London sits at 1.20 and Dubai at 1.10 to 1.15, a figure that misleads: with no income tax, a nominal Dubai base of USD 141,000 comfortably exceeds a Geneva base of USD 179,000 after deductions.

The market tightened sharply after late 2024. Demand for certified protective personnel rose 75 per cent year on year, ad hoc travel security by 300 per cent, and median per-executive security spend moved from USD 69,000 to USD 94,000 a year. The ASIS executive protection standard published in September 2025 explicitly recommends that the director of security should not personally stand a close-protection post, the two disciplines being distinct. Mature programmes now separate the functions cleanly.

The point of contact with the rest of the house is constant. The director of security reports to the chief of staff in 45 per cent of programmes, to a family office director in 30 per cent, and directly to the principal in 25 per cent. Vendor access control, background vetting of household staff and training the team on confidentiality protocols all sit inside that daily coordination. Non-disclosure agreements are standard before hire, and firms prefer candidates with no social media presence.
lead.why: Security and household service now share the same corridors, the same rosters and often the same line manager. Reading a protective headcount, a rotation pattern and a confidentiality clause is part of the estate manager's job.
lead.src: Talent Gurus, Executive Protection Salary Guide 2026

articles.title: The wealthy family stops choosing a country and starts assembling a portfolio of jurisdictions
articles.body:
The 2026 Henley & Partners report on private wealth migration abandons the logic of inflow and outflow league tables for a framework that scores jurisdictions across twelve dimensions and thirty-eight weighted indicators. Its central finding is that the most mobile families no longer pick a destination country. They build what the report calls a sovereign portfolio, combining residence rights, citizenships, investment structures and education options spread across several jurisdictions.

The demand figures give the measure of it. In the first five months of 2026 the firm received applications from 86 nationalities across 47 investment migration programmes. More than 28 per cent of applicants already live outside their country of nationality. The stated objective is not departure but distribution, so that no single government holds the whole of a family's life and capital.

The competitiveness ranking puts Singapore first at 79.5 out of 100, ahead of New Zealand at 75.8, then the Cayman Islands, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Portugal, Italy and Bermuda. The United Arab Emirates score 85.3, among the highest in the framework, despite regional tensions. At the other end, Germany at 69.7, Norway at 69.0, the United Kingdom at 68.3 and France at 65.7 are classed as competitive jurisdictions under pressure.

Application flows confirm those positions. Applications from UK addresses rose 15 per cent between 2024 and 2025, and British citizens now account for almost half of all applications originating in the UK, against 8 per cent in 2018. Applications from US nationals doubled in 2025 and remain elevated in 2026, with only 7 per cent coming from Americans living abroad. The firm recorded a 16 per cent rise in enquiries from German nationals between Q4 2025 and Q1 2026, and France moved from its top 40 source nationalities in 2024 to its top 15 in 2026.

The Gulf case deserves precise reading. Enquiries from UAE-based individuals rose 41 per cent between Q4 2025 and Q1 2026, and applications for alternative residence or citizenship by 29 per cent. The report reads this as diversification and contingency planning, driven by expatriate entrepreneurs and internationally mobile families using the country as a base, rather than as an exodus.
articles.why: A family spread across four jurisdictions does not want the same service four times over. It wants staff who can track tax presence calendars, distinct employment law regimes and houses that open and close in rotation.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

articles.title: The global ultra wealthy class now numbers 556,850 people
articles.body:
Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026 puts the global ultra high net worth population, defined from USD 30m in net worth, at 556,850 individuals, an all-time high. Growth reached 14.4 per cent across 2025, the strongest since 2017, and marks a second consecutive year of double-digit expansion. Over two years the population has grown by almost 30 per cent, adding more than 120,000 people.

Combined wealth in this group stands at USD 63.8 trillion, more than double the annual GDP of the United States. Concentration is the striking feature: the ultra wealthy make up 1.1 per cent of the global millionaire population yet command 32 per cent of its cumulative wealth. North America, Asia and Europe are home to more than 90 per cent of the class.

The regional dynamic is shifting. Asia recorded 15.8 per cent growth in its ultra wealthy population in 2025 and is forecast to post the strongest expansion of the three major regions to 2030. Altrata projects a global population of 746,570 individuals by then, with combined wealth of USD 85 trillion, a third larger than the 2025 level.

What these numbers describe, seen from private service, is not a statistical abstraction. Each crossing of the USD 30m threshold corresponds, statistically, to a household that acquires one or more additional residences, structures a family office, or delegates the running of its domestic life to someone else. The pool of positions follows that curve with a lag of a few years.
articles.why: The number of houses that need running tracks the number of fortunes crossing the thirty million line. It is the most reliable base for sizing the private service job market.

articles.title: Charter booking lead times fall from 118 days to 83
articles.body:
Booking data through the end of May describes a charter market where the decision is being taken much closer to departure. Average booking lead time has fallen from 118 days in 2025 to 83 days in 2026, a reduction of almost 30 per cent year on year. It is the clearest shift in booking behaviour observed this season.

The compression in timing is striking. Nearly one third of forward June 2026 bookings were for charters beginning in June itself, and more than 60 per cent for departures before the end of July. Of 1,162 forward bookings recorded in June, 939, or 80.8 per cent, were for charters taking place between June and August. Brokers read this less as a lasting change in habit than as a response to geopolitical uncertainty, with clients reluctant to commit far ahead.

The geography, by contrast, has not moved. The Western Mediterranean, Eastern Mediterranean and Adriatic account for almost 80 per cent of forward June bookings, the Western Mediterranean alone representing 546 bookings, close to half the month's activity. Athens remains the leading embarkation point with 161 bookings, ahead of Nice with 53 and Monaco with 46.

Charter length is edging up. Median duration moved from seven days in June 2025 to eight days in June 2026, and the eight to ten day band has become the largest booking category with 499 bookings, or 42.9 per cent of activity. The traditional week has lost first place. For crew, a preparation window shortened by 35 days combined with longer voyages mechanically changes the rhythm of provisioning, relief hiring and itinerary planning.
articles.why: An order book that fills three weeks before departure forces crew and shore-side concierges to hold supply chains and itineraries ready without visibility. That is a skill of anticipation, not of reaction.

articles.title: The collector car market splits in two, a top that holds and a middle that gives way
articles.body:
The collector car market in 2026 shows an unusual gap between its summit and its body. Hagerty's Blue Chip Index, tracking the most sought-after pieces, sits at 75.54, while the Hagerty Hundred, a weighted average of condition number 2 values across the hundred most insured vehicles, has slipped to 48.32. Nearly twenty-seven points separate the two measures.

The Hagerty Hundred peaked in May 2022 above USD 50,000 in average value. It now stands at USD 43,408 and, adjusted for inflation, is at an all-time low. Hagerty's broader Market Index has gained ground for three consecutive months to 172.5, but the Market Rating has trended lower for six months and the auction median sale price has set a fresh low in real terms.

The practical reading of that gap is simple. Rare, documented pieces continue to clear seven figures, while good driver-quality classics have become markedly easier to buy. The market is not falling, it is polarising, and original documentation and service history are what decide which side of the line a car falls on.

The Monterey sales in August draw the deepest pool of high-end buyers in the world. They will show whether the strength at the top observed in the first half carries into the autumn. For a house holding a collection garage, the interval is precisely when insured value and market value can diverge significantly by segment.
articles.why: A collection garage is an inventory and insurance line managed through files, not memories. A polarised market makes maintenance history decisive for value.

articles.title: In Meursault, ten rooms built around the winemaker's craft
articles.body:
Maison Le Chevreuil opens this July in Meursault, one of the most celebrated villages of the Côte de Beaune, with ten rooms designed around the art of winemaking. The format is that of the small Burgundian village house rather than the destination hotel, in a commune whose entire reputation rests on its whites.

The choice of location says something about the moment. Meursault is not a resort, it is a working wine village where access to the domaines runs through relationships rather than reservations. A ten-room house that settles there is addressing guests who have come to understand an appellation, not to be seen.

For a private concierge, this is precisely the kind of address that gains value in a contacts book. Requests for Burgundy tastings run into a severely constrained supply of domaines, where visits cannot be bought and an introduction counts for more than a budget. A well-run local base within walking distance of the cellars is a more useful lever than a palace hotel a hundred kilometres away.
articles.why: Cultural fluency in wine is judged on the ability to secure a visit where visits are not sold. Knowing the village addresses of Burgundy is worth more than a directory of grand hotels.

briefs.t: Business aviation advances, except in the Middle East
briefs.b: Global business jet activity rose 3.9 per cent across the first half of 2026, and 2.7 per cent in June alone. North America gained 4.6 per cent and Africa 5.2 per cent, while Europe slipped 0.5 per cent. The rest of the world fell 2.6 per cent, driven by a 15 per cent contraction in the Middle East.

briefs.t: The rarest post in private security
briefs.b: The technical surveillance counter-measures specialist, responsible for detecting listening devices, cameras and trackers in residences and private aircraft, carries a scarcity rating of 10 out of 10. The US pool holds 12 to 40 candidates, every one trained in a government counter-intelligence school, with no civilian pipeline. Time to fill runs to 24 weeks for a median salary of USD 140,000.

briefs.t: Delhi leads ultra wealthy growth to 2030
briefs.b: Altrata forecasts Delhi as the fastest-growing city by ultra wealthy population to 2030, followed by Stockholm and Wuhan. The projection carries the global population to 746,570 individuals holding USD 85 trillion. The new maps of private service recruitment are being drawn along these urban trajectories.

briefs.t: Greece and Italy capture the redirected demand
briefs.b: Greece, scored at 70.5 in the Henley 2026 framework, is among the clearest beneficiaries of Spain's golden visa closure and Portugal's withdrawal of its real estate route. Italy, at 72.3, is drawing on its flat-tax regime for new residents and its inheritance framework, with Milan establishing itself as a family office centre. When a government closes a pathway, demand does not disappear, it relocates.

lead.title: Dubaï signe un record de maisons au dessus de dix millions, pendant que Londres vide les siennes
lead.standfirst: Le premier semestre 2026 a produit 296 ventes résidentielles à plus de dix millions de dollars à Dubaï, au moment où deux tiers des vendeurs super prime londoniens quittent le pays.
lead.body:
Le premier semestre 2026 s'est refermé à Dubaï sur 296 ventes de résidences au dessus de dix millions de dollars, pour un cumul de 5,1 milliards de dollars. La valeur progresse de 14 pour cent sur un an et le nombre de transactions de 16 pour cent par rapport au premier semestre 2025. Comparé au premier semestre 2024, la hausse atteint 49 pour cent. Aucune autre place n'a produit une accélération comparable sur la même période.

La géographie de ces ventes est concentrée. Dubai Hills Estate mène le classement avec 51 ventes au dessus de dix millions, Palm Jumeirah suit avec 50. La transaction la plus élevée du semestre porte sur un appartement de six chambres aux Aman Residences, à Jumeirah Second, cédé pour 114,9 millions de dollars. Ce sont des adresses de résidence principale ou de seconde base durable, pas des placements de passage, et elles arrivent avec une exigence de personnel et de logistique domestique.

À l'échelle mondiale, Knight Frank a recensé 636 transactions résidentielles au dessus de dix millions de dollars au premier trimestre, pour 11,4 milliards de dollars, le meilleur trimestre en un an. Dubaï, Hong Kong et New York mènent le volume, Londres remonte au quatrième rang. Le haut du marché se comporte donc à l'inverse du reste, puisque les prix du marché grand public de Dubaï reculent de 5 à 20 pour cent selon les quartiers, à mesure que des propriétaires et des investisseurs sortent.

Le mouvement londonien est de sens inverse et tout aussi structurant. Environ 65 pour cent des vendeurs super prime de la capitale britannique sont des non doms qui cèdent leur résidence principale pour s'installer ailleurs, principalement à Dubaï, Abou Dabi, Milan, en Toscane, à Monaco et à Genève. Beauchamp Estates anticipe un tassement supplémentaire de 2 à 3 pour cent des valeurs super prime londoniennes sur 2026, surtout là où l'offre reste abondante ou près des seuils de taxation foncière évoqués.

Le résultat est une carte de la richesse qui se redessine par les murs plutôt que par les déclarations fiscales. Une maison ouverte au Golfe et une maison fermée à Londres ne s'annulent pas, elles créent deux chantiers de gestion distincts, avec deux calendriers, deux droits du travail et deux cultures de service.
lead.why: Chaque vente au dessus de dix millions correspond à une maison à ouvrir, à équiper et à doter en personnel, ou à une maison à fermer, à archiver et à mettre sous garde. Le marché des adresses commande directement le marché des postes.

articles.title: Le chef privé atteint trois cent mille dollars, et le recrutement se prépare six mois à l'avance
articles.body:
Le rapport annuel 2026 de Morgan & Mallet sur le personnel de maison place quatre fonctions en tête de la demande aux États-Unis : gouvernante, chef privé, nurse ou nanny, et estate manager. La hiérarchie est stable depuis plusieurs cycles, mais les conditions d'accès à ces postes se sont nettement déplacées vers le haut.

Les rémunérations en témoignent. Les meilleurs chefs privés américains atteignent désormais 300 000 dollars par an. Les nannies employées par des ménages ultra fortunés se situent de 95 000 à 170 000 dollars, les niveaux supérieurs allant aux profils de carrière qui couvrent plusieurs résidences ou accompagnent la famille en déplacement international. Ce sont des grilles de cadre, plus des grilles de service domestique, et elles s'accompagnent d'attentes de disponibilité et de discrétion équivalentes.

La demande de chefs privés est très concentrée géographiquement. Les États-Unis représentent 35 pour cent des placements, les Émirats et le Moyen-Orient 20 pour cent, la France et Monaco 20 pour cent également. Un candidat mobile sur ces trois zones se rend donc éligible à environ trois quarts du marché mondial de la fonction.

Le calendrier de recrutement s'est allongé. Les familles sont invitées à prévoir de 4 à 6 mois pour une embauche, contre 2 à 3 mois auparavant, faute de candidats qualifiés disponibles. Les qualifications qui font la différence se sont aussi spécialisées : formation en nutrition pour les chefs, profil scientifique ou STEM pour les nannies. La compétence de base ne suffit plus à emporter une place, elle sert de ticket d'entrée.
articles.why: Le délai de recrutement de quatre à six mois signifie qu'une candidature bien préparée entre dans un processus long, où la spécialisation documentée pèse davantage que la disponibilité immédiate.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet, Household Staff Industry Report 2026

articles.title: Cent vingt quatre mille milliards changent de mains, et la maison n'a presque jamais été préparée
articles.body:
Le transfert de patrimoine intergénérationnel américain est estimé à 124 000 milliards de dollars par Bank of America Private Bank, avec des transmissions annuelles qui approcheraient 5 000 milliards à l'horizon 2048. À l'échelle mondiale, environ 83 000 milliards de dollars devraient changer de mains sur les deux prochaines décennies. Les estimations varient fortement selon la méthode retenue, de 36 000 milliards à plus de 100 000 milliards, ce qui dit surtout que personne ne mesure exactement le phénomène qu'il annonce.

La répartition générationnelle est plus lisible. La génération X devrait hériter d'environ 14 000 milliards de dollars sur dix ans, les millennials d'environ 46 000 milliards sur vingt cinq ans, soit près de 18 000 milliards pour les deux groupes réunis sur la seule prochaine décennie. Le pouvoir de décision domestique va donc passer à des personnes qui ont aujourd'hui de 30 à 61 ans.

La nature des actifs transmis change aussi. Bank of America relève qu'en 2026 la part des entreprises héritées parmi les Américains fortunés atteint 23 pour cent, contre 11 pour cent d'entreprises achetées, inversant un rapport historiquement favorable à l'acquisition. Une entreprise familiale héritée s'accompagne le plus souvent d'un patrimoine immobilier et d'une organisation domestique héritée avec elle.

La préparation, elle, reste faible. Le Global Next Generation Report 2026 d'UBS, qui a interrogé plus de 170 héritiers, constate que près de la moitié d'entre eux déclarent qu'aucun transfert structuré n'a été organisé par la génération précédente. Du côté des détenteurs, 79 pour cent associent leurs conseillers aux discussions successorales, mais seuls 36 pour cent jugent leurs héritiers très préparés, et 61 pour cent s'inquiètent de l'effet de la richesse sur la motivation personnelle de leurs enfants.
articles.why: Un changement de génération à la tête d'une maison redéfinit les priorités, les usages et souvent l'équipe. La personne qui connaît les procédures et l'histoire de la maison devient l'élément de continuité le plus difficile à remplacer.
articles.src: Fortune, Bank of America Private Bank, UBS

articles.title: La rotation descend vers les quarante mètres, et l'équipage devient le vrai goulot d'étranglement
articles.body:
La flotte mondiale compte 6 423 unités et environ 340 livraisons de plus de 30 mètres sont attendues sur l'année. Chaque coque neuve entre en service avec un équipage complet à constituer, ce qui place la contrainte non plus sur le chantier mais sur le vivier humain disponible.

Les rémunérations ont suivi. Les salaires d'équipage ont progressé de 8 à 12 pour cent depuis 2023, sous l'effet combiné de la pénurie et de l'inflation. Un poste d'entrée se situe de 2 000 à 3 500 euros par mois, avec une progression rapide dès l'acquisition de brevets et d'ancienneté à bord. Un capitaine de grande unité se situe de 10 000 à 16 000 euros par mois, davantage sur les plus gros programmes. La tension est particulièrement forte sur les machines, les officiers pont et les postes rotatifs.

Le changement structurel est ailleurs. La rotation, c'est à dire le congé programmé avec un remplaçant identifié, était historiquement réservée aux très grandes unités. Elle est désormais attendue à partir des yachts de 40 à 50 mètres. Un armateur qui ne l'offre pas se prive d'une part croissante des candidats expérimentés, quel que soit le salaire proposé.

Les recruteurs du secteur convergent sur un constat : la fidélisation ne se joue plus seulement sur la rémunération, mais sur un environnement qui permet de progresser, avec formation financée et perspective de poste. Les hubs de recrutement restent les États-Unis, la Méditerranée et le Moyen-Orient, avec des écarts de niveau croissants entre ces zones.
articles.why: Le yacht et la maison à terre puisent dans le même vivier de personnel de service, avec des standards de rotation et de formation désormais comparables. Ce que la mer concède en congé programmé, la maison finit par devoir l'aligner.

articles.title: L'horlogerie suisse recule de trois pour cent, et c'est le haut de gamme qui encaisse
articles.body:
Après cinq mois, les exportations horlogères suisses affichent un repli cumulé de 3,1 pour cent. Le premier trimestre avait pourtant ouvert en légère hausse, à 6,2 milliards de francs et 1,4 pour cent de progression. Sur quatre mois, le cumul de 8,33 milliards de francs reste globalement stable face à 2024, mais en baisse de 3,9 pour cent face à 2025, année de comparaison élevée.

La carte des marchés se lit clairement. Sur janvier à avril, l'Asie représente 45 pour cent de la valeur exportée, devant l'Europe à 30 pour cent et les Amériques à 22 pour cent. Les États-Unis sont de loin le premier pays destinataire, avec 1,53 milliard de francs importés depuis le début de l'année, près de trois fois le Japon à 583 millions et le Royaume Uni à 534 millions. L'Inde progresse de 39 pour cent à 111,4 millions de francs et se hisse au quinzième rang mondial sur la période.

Le détail par segment est le plus instructif pour une maison qui gère une collection. En avril, les montres exportées à plus de 3 000 francs ont vu leur valeur reculer de 19 pour cent et leurs volumes de 21 pour cent. Le repli ne vient donc pas du bas de gamme mais du segment que possèdent les clients de service privé, dans un marché devenu fragmenté et sélectif.

Un marché qui se contracte par le haut modifie la manière dont les pièces circulent. Les acquisitions ralentissent, les arbitrages augmentent, et les questions de valorisation, d'assurance et de traçabilité des pièces reviennent au premier plan de la gestion domestique.
articles.why: L'inventaire horloger d'une maison n'est pas un décor, c'est un actif assuré dont la valeur bouge. Un segment haut de gamme en repli impose des réévaluations et un suivi documentaire plus serré.
articles.src: Fédération de l'industrie horlogère suisse, WatchPro

articles.title: Aux Açores, cinq villas privées vendues comme une maison, avec le concierge au bout du fil
articles.body:
Residence Azores propose sur São Miguel, la plus grande île de l'archipel, un ensemble de cinq villas de quatre chambres pensées comme des résidences privées plutôt que comme des chambres d'hôtel. Chaque villa dispose d'un balcon avec vue mer, d'un jardin privatif, d'une piscine et d'un bain à remous. Les tarifs commencent à environ 569 dollars la nuit.

Le service est la partie intéressante. Un concierge joignable par WhatsApp organise la venue de chefs privés pour les repas préparés sur place, planifie les activités et les séquences de bien être, des randonnées aux bains thermaux, jusqu'à un massage utilisant les pierres géothermiques de l'île. Le concept a été conçu pour les séjours longs et le travail à distance, sans exclure les courts passages.

Le modèle est révélateur d'un déplacement plus large. L'hôtellerie haut de gamme cesse de vendre une chambre avec des services et vend désormais une maison avec un intendant, c'est à dire exactement le vocabulaire et l'organisation du service privé. Le chef qui vient cuisiner dans la villa, la demande transmise par messagerie, l'agenda tenu pour la famille : ce sont des fonctions de maison, sous marque d'hôtel.
articles.why: Quand l'hôtellerie recrute pour reproduire l'expérience d'une maison privée, elle recrute sur les mêmes compétences que les familles. C'est une porte d'entrée et une concurrence à la fois.

briefs.t: The best half since 2022
briefs.b: Christie's affiche 4,5 milliards de dollars de revenus au premier semestre 2026, dont 3,5 milliards en enchères publiques, en hausse de 71 pour cent sur un an. Sotheby's signe son meilleur semestre historique à 4,4 milliards, avec un record de 826 millions en ventes privées. Les trois grandes maisons cumulent 6,8 milliards, en progression de 70 pour cent.

briefs.t: North America keeps flying
briefs.b: ARGUS relève une activité mondiale d'aviation d'affaires en hausse de 3,4 pour cent en juin sur un an. L'Amérique du Nord progresse de 2,2 pour cent, tirée par le fractionnaire à plus de 10,4 pour cent, tandis que l'Europe recule de 0,5 pour cent et le Moyen Orient de 15 pour cent.

briefs.t: London counts its sellers
briefs.b: Environ 65 pour cent des vendeurs super prime londoniens sont des non doms qui cèdent leur résidence principale pour rejoindre des juridictions moins taxées. Beauchamp Estates anticipe un repli supplémentaire de 2 à 3 pour cent des valeurs super prime en 2026, avec une stabilisation attendue sur les meilleures adresses.

briefs.t: The mobility gap widens
briefs.b: Singapour conserve la première place de l'indice Henley avec 192 destinations accessibles sans visa sur 227. Les Émirats arabes unis sont le plus fort progressiste sur vingt ans, avec 149 destinations gagnées depuis 2006 et 57 places grimpées, pour 184 destinations aujourd'hui. L'écart entre le passeport le plus mobile et le moins mobile atteint 168 destinations.
